claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 4 and subclaim 5, run a causal head-ablation study on a public safety-aligned open-weight chat model under both normal harmful prompts and successful jailbreak prompts. Use a publicly available harmful-instruction set such as AdvBench or HarmBench behaviors, plus a public jailbreak set such as JailbreakBench, and first verify a baseline pattern: the model refuses many direct harmful prompts but complies more often when paired with successful jailbreak wrappers. Then trace per-head attention outputs and activation magnitudes across layers for matched prompt pairs (same harmful request, with and without jailbreak), ranking heads by the size of their activity decrease specifically on jailbreak-success cases relative to direct-refusal cases. Intervene causally by suppressing only the top-k candidate heads during direct harmful prompts, using head output zeroing or mean-replacement, and measure whether refusals convert to compliant harmful answers. As controls, suppress random matched-size head sets, top-k heads chosen from harmless prompts, and candidate heads on benign prompts to estimate specificity and side effects. If suppressing a small identified subset reliably flips refusals to compliance at much higher rates than random/control ablations, that supports the claim that jailbreaks selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads and that suppressing that subset is sufficient to induce compliance. If no small subset can be found, or many unrelated heads must be ablated, that weakens the selective-suppression and sufficiency claims. If stronger direct evidence already existed in the form of published per-head causal intervention results on the same model family and public benchmarks, this experiment could be partly unnecessary or reduced to replication.

To address subclaim 1, subclaim 2, subclaim 3, and subclaim 6, test whether safety-relevant harmfulness representations persist during successful jailbreaks rather than disappearing. Using the same public model and prompt sets, collect hidden states and attention-head outputs for four conditions: benign prompts, direct harmful prompts that elicit refusal, harmful prompts with unsuccessful jailbreaks, and harmful prompts with successful jailbreaks. Define a readout direction for harmfulness without extra training by using simple activation differencing from the model’s own internal contrast: for example, compute layerwise mean activation differences between harmful and benign prompts on a held-out split, or use token-level contrasts around refusal-triggering positions. Then evaluate whether this unsupervised harmfulness signal remains high on successful jailbreak cases even when the final behavior is compliant, and localize which heads/layers still carry it. In parallel, check whether the specific heads identified in Experiment 1 lose the signal while many other heads retain it. If harmfulness-related signals remain robust in non-suppressed heads during successful jailbreaks, that supports the bypass-not-elimination account; if the signal broadly collapses across the network on successful jailbreaks, that would favor elimination instead. If only the candidate suppressed heads lose signal while many others keep encoding harmfulness, that strongly supports selective bypass. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already strong public mechanistic evidence showing layer/head-level harmfulness probes stay separable on jailbreak-success examples across multiple models.

To address subclaim 7, subclaim 8, and subclaim 9, evaluate whether the persistent internal representations can be used directly as a competitive harmful-input detector without additional training. Using the representations identified in Experiment 2, construct zero-shot or training-free detectors from public benchmark prompts: for instance, score each input by cosine similarity to a harmfulness prototype vector, by projection onto the unsupervised harmful-minus-benign direction, or by aggregating activations from heads/layers shown to retain harmfulness information. Evaluate on public datasets with harmful and benign inputs, such as HarmBench, AdvBench, BeaverTails, and XSTest or SafeBench-style harmless challenge sets if publicly available, including jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompts. Compare AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at a chosen threshold, and calibration against dedicated public safety baselines such as open moderation models or simple trained classifiers available on HuggingFace. Strictly avoid fitting any new detector parameters beyond threshold selection on a validation split, so the test addresses the no-additional-training claim. If a training-free internal detector is competitive with dedicated safety models, especially on jailbreak examples, that supports the readout and competitiveness claims; if it lags substantially or requires learned probe weights to work well, those claims weaken. This experiment could be made unnecessary if existing public evaluations already showed a no-training internal activation score matching or exceeding established safety classifiers on the same benchmarks.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 uses the same harmful request in direct-refusal and successful-jailbreak conditions, collects layerwise hidden states and head outputs, and explicitly tests whether the internal harmfulness signal remains high or collapses during successful compliance. Its signal is constructed differently from the reference refusal direction, but it has the same discriminating power for the claim's persistence-versus-elimination question.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired behavioral dataset in which the same harmful request is refused without an attack and succeeds with an attack, allowing attack effects to be separated from differences in request content.

Proposed experiment 0 uses whole-prompt activity changes and proposed experiment 1 uses whole representations and head localization; proposed experiment 2 uses those representations for readout, but none performs the token/template decomposition.
Whole-prompt suppression and persistence results can therefore be explained either by selective bypass or by differing sensitivity to the content and form of the complete prompt.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the observed head specialization is specific to the jailbreak template rather than to harmful-content sensitivity.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external test of a training-free internal readout across varied safety data, including jailbreak-wrapped inputs, with comparable classification metrics and direct comparison to dedicated safety systems, establishing both usefulness and competitive quality.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 constructs zero-shot/training-free activation readouts, permits only validation threshold selection, evaluates multiple harmful/benign and jailbreak-relevant public resources, and compares AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and calibration with public moderation or other dedicated safety baselines. This is sufficient for the claim about whether such a detector can be competitive for the evaluated safety-aligned model; the reference's exact benchmark count and multi-family model breadth are not binding where the claim does not name them. The proposed resources are publicly obtainable (E0-E4), and a proposed model of the required general kind is obtainable subject to access terms (E5).

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would establish persistence, identify and causally test a selectively suppressible head subset, and evaluate a training-free detector against safety baselines. It would not settle the full mechanistic claim because it lacks the token-level request-versus-jailbreak-template attribution needed to distinguish bypass from the harmful-content-sensitivity rival, and it only partially tests whether the other retaining heads are causally responsible for the residual signal.
missing: Token-level attribution separating original harmful-request tokens from jailbreak-template tokens and comparing the candidate and retaining head populations on those sources.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched-condition, layer- and component-level comparison that tests whether a safety-relevant internal signal remains on successful jailbreaks rather than disappearing from the network.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 compares direct harmful refusals with successful jailbreak cases for matched harmful requests, collects hidden states and head outputs across layers, constructs a training-free harmfulness signal, and explicitly tests whether it remains high and where it is carried. That can establish persistence versus broad collapse without requiring the reference's particular refusal-direction statistic.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired evaluation population containing the same harmful requests in refused and successful-jailbreak conditions, so attack effects can be separated from differences in request content.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 verifies the direct-refusal versus successful-wrapper behavior on public harmful and jailbreak material, while experiment 1 explicitly uses matched prompt pairs and separates successful from unsuccessful jailbreaks. The named resources are publicly discoverable (E0, E1), and the claim does not bind the study to the reference's particular attack algorithms or pair count.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level procedure for identifying a small attack-associated subset of heads, distinguishing it from controls well enough to support a causal test.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 ranks heads by jailbreak-specific activity decrease, examines the ranking across k, and tests candidate sets against random, harmless-prompt, and benign-prompt controls. This is a different but directly discriminating identification instrument from the reference's projection and overlap thresholds; threshold and bandwidth sweeps are not required by the claim when the candidate selection is tested causally and against matched controls.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention on only the identified small subset, with matched-size controls, that measures conversion of a normally refused harmful request into compliant output.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 directly suppresses top-k candidate heads during direct harmful prompts, measures refusal-to-compliance conversion, and includes random matched-size and other specificity/side-effect controls. Zeroing or mean replacement is an adequate suppression intervention; the reference's particular feature-injection implementation and seed count are not claim requirements.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct measurement that heads outside the selectively affected subset still encode harmful content during successful jailbreaks, with comparisons to refused or unattacked conditions.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 records head outputs and hidden states in matched direct-refusal and successful-jailbreak conditions, localizes the retained signal, and explicitly tests whether noncandidate heads continue to carry it. This answers the representational persistence question even without repeating the reference's separate suppression-of-the-other-head-type intervention.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates responses to the original harmful request from responses to the jailbreak template, allowing the selective-bypass account to be distinguished from a simple difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed matched prompts and head-level traces get at whether changes are associated with adding a jailbreak wrapper, but they do not attribute each head's activation to request tokens versus wrapper tokens or compare the two head groups on those token classes. Thus a whole-prompt activity difference could still reflect unequal harmful-content sensitivity, leaving the mechanistic rival explanation unresolved.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 distinguishes the bypass account from a sensitivity-only account by separately measuring contributions from harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 1 compare matched whole prompts and rank or read out aggregate head activity, but perform no token-level attribution.
[3] A head-level difference between the two prompt conditions can therefore be caused either by attack-template processing or by different sensitivity to the harmful content itself.

[4] The team would learn that candidate heads behave differently under successful wrappers, but would fail to learn whether the head types are indistinguishable on harmful-request tokens and diverge specifically on template tokens.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external, held-out quantitative evaluation of a training-free internal readout across varied safety data, including jailbreak cases, against dedicated safety-model baselines.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 constructs zero-shot/training-free activation readouts, permits only validation threshold selection, evaluates multiple public harmful/benign and jailbreak-containing datasets with several standard metrics, and compares against public safety baselines. The claim requires competitiveness for a qualifying safety-aligned model, not the reference's exact number of models, architecture families, or benchmarks. The proposed external resources are discoverable (E0-E2).
